GHrmKL2XKcE.why: Shared for insight into how taste drives practice and creative development.

p.x:
Taste is a measure of how far you can see without scaffolding. 

The more taste you have, the less scaffolding you need, and vice-versa. 

Those who can see further away, can win by building the scaffolding needed to bring what they see within reach of those who can't yet see it. https://t.co/ECmu7M9s00

comments.x: @geoffreylitt Reminds me of ira glass’ piece on the creative process / taste gap! https://t.co/GzPwLZO7p0

p.x:
I’ve noticed people who have good creative ideas usually know tons of things.

Good researchers have read a lot of papers. Good musicians have listened to a lot of songs.

Not only that, they generally have strong opinions about what’s good/bad out there. 

I wonder why?

I strongly suspect a causal relationship that goes something like this: “Everything is a remix”, so having good raw ingredients in your head enables good output.

In fact, in some domains I’d argue that getting the prereqs into your head is the hardest step! Much of a PhD is getting to the starting line: ingesting enough prior work to have a chance at original contributions. 

There’s also taste. Good taste comes from sampling tons of things and understanding what you like and don’t like. So there’s a volume of input needed to develop it.

But it’s hard to say for sure! I could imagine other explanations contributing.  

Maybe people who naturally produce good ideas just happen to be the same kinds of people who devour lots of inputs? Maybe there’s just a general correlation between memory and intelligence or something?

Of course, knowing stuff doesn’t automatically imply having good ideas. But it does seem to me that smart/talented people are often bottlenecked on  knowledge and experience more than anything else…

p.x:
I'm confused by what to do about "synchronicities"

Like this morning I googled whether the final Name of the Wind book has a release date (no)

Then I saw a woman reading the Name of the Wind on the subway and we struck up a geeky conversation

Then, in a bookstore, Lin-Manuel Miranda was reading something behind me. Lin-Manuel Miranda was tapped to produce and compose for the Name of the Wind movie trilogy and TV show

My woo friends & Jung fans would interpret this sort of thing as very meaningful, perhaps a message from the universe. I interpret this sort of thing as the Baader–Meinhof phenomenon, a cognitive bias where you notice something and then it seems to appear everywhere

But let's say I treat these things as messages from the universe. Would that make my life any better? I feel like I'd just get whipped around by random patterns

Maybe I'll spend a week living the "synchronicities are real and important" lifestyle and see what happens
